analysis.investment_thesis: Alembic is a century-old Indian pharma franchise with high promoter conviction (69.74%) and decent gross margins, but a decade of capital-intensive expansion has destroyed shareholder value — net profit CAGR of -2.3% over 9 years tells the whole story. I need to see two or three years of sustained earnings recovery and ROE crossing 15% before getting excited here.
key_strengths: High promoter holding at 69.74% — skin in the game, aligned with minority shareholders
Strong gross margins at 71.51% signal genuine product pricing power in branded generics
Manageable D/E of 0.28 and 5/5 years of positive OCF historically show financial discipline
key_risks: Earnings destruction: net profit collapsed from peak INR 1,146 Cr (FY21) to INR 582 Cr (FY25) — still 49% below peak after 4 years
FY25 cash flow crisis: OCF crashed to just INR 88 Cr vs INR 803 Cr in FY24, FCF turned negative at -466 Cr, while borrowings nearly tripled from INR 513 Cr to INR 1,489 Cr in a single year
Capital intensity trap: another capex cycle beginning (CWIP up to INR 903 Cr) before the last cycle (peak CWIP INR 2,304 Cr in FY22) has delivered adequate returns
red_flags: Finance costs growing at 35.9% CAGR — from INR 5 Cr to INR 79 Cr — eating into profitability
ROE of 11.4% and ROCE of 13% are well below my 15% minimum threshold — capital destruction at current reinvestment rates
EBITDA CAGR of -0.3% over 9 years means the company earned more operating profit in 2016 than in 2025 despite doubling revenue
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Alembic is a cautionary tale of a good business that over-invested. The massive CWIP build (peak INR 2,304 Cr in FY22) was supposed to transform the company into a US generics powerhouse, but US pricing pressure crushed margins just as capacity came online. Revenue grew at a respectable 8.6% CAGR, but operating income is literally flat over 9 years — every rupee of growth was consumed by capex, depreciation, and rising finance costs. Operating margin at 11.37% is mediocre for a pharma company of this vintage.

What alarmed me most is FY25: OCF collapsed to INR 88 Cr (from INR 803 Cr prior year), free cash flow went to -466 Cr, and the company raised borrowings by nearly INR 1,000 Cr in a single year — signaling the new capex cycle is again being funded by debt. At 23x trailing P/E and 18.55x forward P/E, the market is already pricing in a recovery that hasn't materialised. For me to get conviction, I need ROE >15%, sustained OCF generation above INR 600 Cr, and evidence the US generics business is actually delivering — not just hope priced into forward earnings.
